newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower on renewed rate hike fears.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower on renewed rate hike fears.

text.p: Under the weight of strong economic data, U.S. Treasuries ended mostly lower on Wednesday amid renewed fears the Federal Reserve will hike rates at its next policy setting meeting in May.
But after falling more than a half-point early in the session, bond prices rallied late in the day to close with only modest losses.
Late Wednesday, the 30-year bond was at 94-5/32, down 2/32 from Tuesday, while its yield rose to 7.10 percent from 7.09 percent.
The late-day rally was attributed mainly to short-covering, although some players noted light hedge fund buying in bond futures.

"Today's action showed that real money accounts are happy where they are positioned," said a trader at a primary dealership. "The market was mostly driven by speculators in Chicago than real money accounts in New York."
Still, traders said the market retained a bearish tone, evidenced by its non-reaction to weak economic report at the start of the session.

Some said they had figured the market would pick up where it left off on Tuesday and rally after the Commerce Department reported a 6.4 percent decline in housing starts in March to a 1.425 million annual unit rate. That was well below expectations of a 1.46 million rate.

But Treasuries ignored the data and instead dove after the Fed said industrial production jumped a higher than expected 0.9 percent in March, with the capacity utilization rate rising to 84.1 percent.
"The reaction to industrial production was justifiable," said David Greenlaw, economist at Morgan Stanley & Co.
"It's confirming evidence on strains in the product market reinforcing on concerns of the labor market," he said. "Everything points to more Fed tightening to slow things down."

Indeed, Fed vice chair Alice Rivlin, in a Market News interview, said she voted for a rate hike in March, but was not sure about whether further rate hikes were needed to cool the economy. However, Rivlin said the economy is growing "faster than is sustainable," leading market analysts to believe Rivlin and the rest of the Fed Board will vote to raise rates again at its May 20 meeting.

Activity was brisk in the morning, but slowed considerably in the afternoon. According to GovPX, volume was 21 percent above average by midday, but by the end of the day, it had slowed to just 12 percent above an average Wednesday in the second quarter of 1996.
Volume, according to GovPX, was nearly $94 billion by 1645 EDT/2045 GMT.
Traders said that shortly after after the production data were released, dealers set up short positions, that were squeezed in the afternoon.

Players said the market should remain under pressure for the next few sessions amid new supply concerns. Wednesday, the Treasury announced it will sell $17 billion two-year notes and $12.5 billion five-year notes next week.
On Thursday, the Labor Department will release weekly jobless claims, while Commerce's February U.S. international trade report is due -- both at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
At 1000 EDT, the Philadelphia Fed's April Business Outlook Survey is due.
Meanwhile, the front end of the market outperformed the rest of the curve, largely due to reinventsment from about $50 billion cash management bills maturing in the next few days.
Bill rates were one basis point lower to one basis point higher.

As for the coupons, the two-year note ended the session at 99-20/32, down 1/32, to yield 6.46 percent. The five-year note was down 2/32 at 99-12/32 to yield 6.78 percent and the 10-year note was down 2/32 at 95-16/32 to yield 6.89 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
